title: Centralized Credential Management for Automation
summary: Centralized credential management for automation tools reviewed for 2026. Compare options to pick the right platform for your team's API keys and secrets.
body_markdown:
## Where Activepieces Fits Credential Management


Activepieces stores a connection once, scopes it to a project, and lets every workflow in that project reuse it; global connections, which are shared beyond one project, come with the Team plan at $200 a month for 25 users.


The controls that let an admin see and revoke across projects are only partly confirmed. That's why the shared token pasted into a separate tool is the case to test it against.


### What the docs confirm


In Activepieces, a connection is its own object, separate from any single workflow. A flow picks the connection by name, so the token is entered once and not copied into each step.


The core is MIT-licensed and public on GitHub, so how a flow resolves a connection can be read in the code rather than taken on trust.


When it expires, you re-authenticate that one connection and every flow that uses it recovers. For the shared-token problem, that's the core of the answer.


Ask who owns a connection and the project answers. The admin page below lists each project with its active users, active flows, and a count of global connections.


Read that last column first when you audit: a global connection is shared beyond one project, so its owner is the person you need to name before anything else.


Look at the screenshot, which shows a single "Company Project" with two global connections.


The page also notes that personal projects are created automatically for new users on signup, which means every new user starts with a space where they can add their own connections. Those are credentials you didn't provision.


Activepieces can send the secrets behind a connection, API keys and OAuth tokens included, to your own secret manager instead of its database, on a self-hosted instance or the enterprise cloud tier.


Secret manager integration is listed on the Ultimate plan, which is sold through sales, alongside SCIM, custom RBAC and audit logs.


Point a self-hosted instance at an external secret manager and the credentials are absent when you inspect the database, so no vendor, Activepieces included, holds the token that expired in this story.


Zapier and Make keep credentials in their own cloud, and neither has a self-hosted edition to route around that. MoneyGram, Moneypenny, Alan and FundingSocieties run Activepieces in production, on an MIT-licensed core with 25,670 GitHub stars.


### What is not confirmed or sits on paid plans


I couldn't confirm from Activepieces' public pages the exact scope of rotation. SSO and standard roles come with the Team plan at $200 a month, while audit logs and custom RBAC are listed on the Ultimate plan, priced through sales.


I couldn't confirm whether the logs record who read or changed a connection, or whether the roles separate using a connection from editing it.


I haven't verified which admin and governance features are tied to paid or enterprise editions, though some are. Pricing and plan limits were checked against the vendor's pages on 2026-11-22 and can change, so ask for the current plan matrix in writing.


Rotation is the clearest gap. Re-authenticating one connection is manual, and I found no documented scheduled rotation or expiry alert.


### Who should pick it and who should not


Pick it if your team wants open-source workflow software, a choice between hosting it yourself or paying for hosted, and connections organised by project with a clear owner. It suits a small group that can name who owns each credential.


Look elsewhere if you need documented audit trails, enforced rotation schedules, or a vault integration you can verify before purchase. Until the vendor confirms those controls in writing, a platform that publishes them is the safer pick.
